title: Metta as a subject
hookLine: bandits demand one of four people, and the manual's answer is: nobody, not even yourself
tomorrow: why feel compassion for someone who seems totally fine?

cards: Four people sit together in the Visuddhimagga's story: a monk, someone he loves, someone he barely knows, and someone who can't stand him. Bandits come in and demand one of them, to do him harm.
If the monk thinks, take that one, he has failed. If he thinks, take the stranger, or take my enemy, he has failed. And here's the twist.
If he thinks, take me instead, spare the other three, he has failed too. The manual's answer to who he hands over: nobody. Not even himself.

teach.b: This is what the manual calls breaking down the barriers, and it's where metta, kindness, is headed as a meditation subject. The training starts small and close. First, yourself: may I be happy and free from suffering.
The manual's reason is plain: you are the example you know best, and wishing yourself well shows you what everyone else wants too.
Then someone neutral, the cashier, the neighbor you nod to. Only then the hard one, someone hostile, and if anger flares there, the manual says to go back to the easier people and come again.
The goal is the scene in the story: a heart so even that it won't pick anybody to give up, and won't pick itself either.
Self-sacrifice sounds noble, but here it's still a barrier, a line drawn with you on the wrong side of it.

teach.h: LIKE A MOTHER WITH ONE CHILD.
teach.b: The Metta Sutta gives the picture of where this goes: as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so toward all beings, a heart without limits.
Kindness, then, isn't a mood. It's a practice with steps, and the last step leaves no one out, including you.

how: Loving-kindness meditation is practiced across Buddhist traditions: wishing well first to oneself, then to a dear person, a neutral person and a difficult person, and finally to all beings; Theravada communities also chant the Metta Sutta.

games.q: what does “metta as a subject” mean?
o: kindness made the object of meditation
giving yourself up to save others
a vow to never feel anger again

games.q: the order of kindness — tap the pairs.
p: where the manual says to begin
last, and back off if anger flares
no one handed over, not even you

s: in the manual's story, offering yourself to the bandits breaks the barriers
even that keeps a barrier. the barriers fall when you can't pick anyone, yourself included.
metta practice begins with your worst enemy
it begins with yourself, then someone dear, then someone neutral, and only then someone hostile.
the Metta Sutta compares the boundless heart to a mother protecting her only child
so toward all beings: a heart without limits.

games.q: you're signing a group birthday card for a classmate. you write something warm, then stop at the line for the kid who annoys you. what would breaking the barriers look like?
o: skip that line; they won't care what you write anyway.
the same warm wish you'd write for anyone, that one included.
sign everyone's name but yours, to stay out of it.
games.why: the manual's goal is a heart that picks nobody to leave out, the hard one and you included. same wish, every line.

practice: Say the old wish quietly, out loud if you can: may I be happy and free from suffering. Then the same words for someone dear, then someone you barely know, then someone difficult, a few breaths each.
If the last one sticks, go back to the easier ones and try again.

wordCard.voice: Metta as a subject: kindness made the object of meditation, spread from yourself outward until no one is handed over.

orig.note: Pali: kindness, friendliness, goodwill; the Sanskrit is maitri.

carryVoice: For the road: kindness, the same wish for everyone, with nobody handed over. That's twenty-nine.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 9 (lovingkindness: begin with oneself; then a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person; return to easier persons if resentment arises; breaking down the barriers, with the simile of bandits demanding one of four people)
Sutta Nipata 1.8 (Karaniya Metta Sutta: as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so toward all beings a boundless heart)
